beforeRecord.q: Consider a case in which a deductible makes the customer pay the first part of a covered loss. Why can it reduce moral hazard?
options: It restores some marginal cost of risky behavior to the customer

beforeRecord.q: A competitive industry has 40 identical firms. At a price of $25, each initially supplies 12 units. Higher energy costs reduce each firm’s supply at that price to 9 units. With unchanged market demand and no entry, equilibrium price then rises to $28. At its new MR = MC quantity of 10 units, a firm has ATC $30 and AVC $21. Which assessment is correct?
options: Market supply shifted left; the firm operates with a $20 economic loss
Market supply shifted right; the firm earns $70 economic profit
Market supply shifted left; the firm shuts down because P is below ATC
Market supply stayed fixed; the firm earns $30 economic profit
beforeRecord.feedback: At the original price, industry supply falls from 480 to 360 units, identifying a leftward shift. At the new optimum, profit is (28 - 30) × 10 = -$20; price still exceeds AVC, so the firm operates. A cost shock can raise market price while reducing profit; the profit result requires the stated cost comparison.

beforeRecord.q: Compare two separate cost increases: higher unavoidable fixed rent, or an extra $3 of variable cost on every unit. What would the shutdown-price threshold be under each change, and which change shifts the firm’s short-run supply?
options: About $14 with higher rent and $17 with the variable cost; only the variable cost shifts supply.
About $18 with higher rent and $21 with the variable cost; only the variable cost shifts supply.
About $17 under either change; both changes shift supply equally.
About $14 under either change; neither change shifts supply.
beforeRecord.feedback: Minimum AVC is about $14. Fixed rent changes neither AVC nor MC, so the shutdown threshold and short-run supply stay unchanged. Adding $3 to each unit’s variable cost raises both AVC and MC by $3, moving the threshold to about $17 and shifting supply upward.

afterRecord.q: A competitive firm has a minimum average variable cost of $14. Compare two separate cost increases: higher unavoidable fixed rent, or an extra $3 of variable cost on every unit. What is the shutdown-price threshold under each change, and which change shifts short-run supply?
options: $14 with higher rent and $17 with variable cost; only variable cost shifts supply.
$18 with higher rent and $21 with variable cost; only variable cost shifts supply.
$17 under either change; both changes shift supply.
$14 under either change; neither change shifts supply.
afterRecord.feedback: The shutdown threshold is minimum AVC. Higher fixed rent changes neither AVC nor MC, leaving the threshold at $14. Adding $3 to variable cost per unit raises AVC and MC by $3, so the threshold becomes $17 and short-run supply shifts upward.

before.imageAlt: A $10 minimum wage lies below the restaurant labor-market equilibrium of 4,000 workers at $15 per hour.

before.imageAlt: A nursing monopsony hires 4,000 nurses where MFC equals MRP and pays $20 on labor supply; competition would employ 6,000 at $25.

Labor supply intersects MRP at the competitive outcome of 6,000 nurses and $25 per hour.

before.imageAlt: Nursing labor demand and supply both shift right, increasing equilibrium employment from 4,000 to 8,000 while the wage remains $20.
